strengths: The core idea—dual (row and column) scale factors with a modified Sinkhorn–Knopp iteration to equalize row/column standard deviations—is simple, elegant, and genuinely useful: it requires no calibration data, has near-RTN runtime (1.09x RTN in Tab. 7), and is layer-independent and thus architecture-agnostic.

Evaluation is unusually broad and mostly convincing: Qwen3 0.6B–235B, Llama 2/3, DeepSeek-V2.5 and DeepSeek-V3 (685B), MoE and MLA architectures, calibration-free, NF4-compatibility, and AWQ-combined (A-SINQ) settings, with ablations over tiling, shifts, and auxiliary precision (Fig. 4).

Memory vs. perplexity Pareto analysis (Fig. 3) fairly accounts for auxiliary-parameter overhead across different parameterizations, and flip-rate metrics following Dutta et al. (2024) supplement perplexity.
The empirical comparison of imbalance vs. kurtosis as proxy targets (Fig. 2) is an interesting insight beyond the method itself, showing imbalance is the better target in the dual-scaling setting.

Combination rules with existing methods (ordering of AWQ scaling relative to SINQ normalization in Sec. 2.2.2, absorption of the second scale into activations per Eq. 6) are clearly worked out and practically important.
Code is promised for reproduction.
weaknesses: The central proxy metric—matrix imbalance (Eq. 4)—is justified almost entirely empirically. There is no analysis linking balanced row/column std to lower quantization error in general; the kurtosis comparison is run only on Qwen3-1.7B, so the claim that imbalance is a better proxy rests on a single model.

Headline gains at the practically most relevant 4-bit setting are modest for larger models (e.g., DeepSeek-V2.5: 5.49 -> 5.48 Wiki2 vs. RTN/HQQ; Qwen3-235B: 5.65 -> 5.58), while the striking improvements are concentrated at 3-bit and on small models; the abstract and intro could be read as overstating the general effect.

Several baselines (RTN, Hadamard+RTN, Hadamard+GPTQ) are the authors' own reimplementations (dagger in Tabs. 1, 2, 5), and some strong prior calibration-free/uniform methods are not compared; comparisons against rotated methods (QuaRot, HIGGS) are limited to a partial memory-matched setup (Tab. 11).

No end-to-end inference throughput or kernel-level latency results are reported; only memory and quantization time. Since the paper argues uncalibrated uniform quantization is preferable for deployment, demonstrating actual inference speedup (not just the 4x memory-bound argument) would substantially strengthen the claims.
A-SINQ modifies the AWQ objective (2-norm to 1-norm, footnote 1), so gains of A-SINQ over AWQ conflate the SINQ contribution with this unexplained objective change; no ablation isolates the effect.

Limitations are not explicitly discussed (e.g., sensitivity to hyperparameters like niter, sigma_min clipping, applicability to attention/output layers beyond linear layers, interaction with quantized auxiliary values in the calibration-free default), which weakens reproducibility and honest scoping of the contribution.

strengths: The core idea is simple and elegant: adding a second-axis scale vector and normalizing row/column standard deviations via a modified Sinkhorn-Knopp iteration is cheap, layer-independent, and architecture-agnostic, and Eq. 6 shows the runtime overhead can be made comparable to AWQ.

The evaluation is broad in model coverage (Qwen3 0.6B-235B, Llama, DeepSeek-V2.5/V3, MoE, MLA) and metric coverage (WikiText2/C4 perplexity, flip rates following Dutta et al. 2024, reasoning traces in Tab. 6), which strengthens external validity beyond a single benchmark.

The method is fast: quantization time is essentially RTN-level (1.09x on average, Tab. 7), so the accuracy gains come at almost no quantization-time cost, and the calibration-free setting genuinely avoids the compute burden of GPTQ/AWQ.

Compatibility ablations are sensible: the paper shows SINQ composes with AWQ calibration (Tab. 5) and NF4 levels (Tab. 4), and analyzes tiling, shifts, and auxiliary precision via Pareto fronts (Fig. 4), treating memory overheads fairly.
Code release is promised and implementation details (group size, tile size, log-domain accumulation, clipping, early stopping) are described concretely.
weaknesses: The headline claim that an uncalibrated uniform quantizer 'can approach the end-to-end output quality of calibrated quantizers or non-uniform formats' is only weakly supported at the practically relevant 4-bit setting. In Tab. 1 and Tab. 5, 4-bit gains over baselines are small (e.g., 8.76 vs. 8.78 for HQQ and 8.85 for Hadamard+RTN on Qwen3-14B), and Fig. 3's own caption concedes the 'maximum distance from the 4-bit pareto front of our method is < 0.01ppl' and that 'the difference to the baseline is small.' The convincing gaps are mostly at 3-bit, where deployment is less common.

Novelty is thinner than presented. Dual per-axis transformations of weight matrices are well explored: DuQuant (Lin et al. 2024a) is literally titled 'dual transformation,' and channel-wise scaling between SmoothQuant/AWQ and this method is an incremental step. The Sinkhorn-Knopp twist (normalizing std devs instead of sums) is a natural modification, yet the paper provides no convergence analysis, no characterization of fixed points of Alg. 1, and no theoretical justification that the matrix imbalance (Eq. 4) is the right proxy for quantization error - the evidence is purely empirical (Fig. 2) and the sigma_min clipping is ad hoc.

Several baselines are self-implemented (marked with daggers in Tabs. 1, 2, 5, 8) without validation against published numbers, and comparisons to some strong related methods are thin or relegated to a single unexplained number (DeepSeek-V3 in Tab. 9, HIGGS only under a special auxiliary-quantization setup in Tab. 11). No uncertainty estimates, seeds, or variance are reported for perplexities despite small differences being used to declare winners.

The stated 'improvements over state-of-the-art baselines' are overstated relative to the evidence: against calibrated GPTQ/AWQ at 4-bit, A-SINQ's advantages are within ~0.05 ppl or a fraction of a flip percentage point (Tabs. 2, 5), well within plausible run-to-run variation.

Presentation has rough edges: incomplete citations (e.g., 'Liu et al.' and 'Akhondzadeh et al.' without venues/years), the abstract's code URL is empty, and the reasoning results are self-described as 'preliminary pass@1' with tiny sample sizes, which sits awkwardly in a submission claiming robust conclusions.

No discussion of failure modes or limitations: the paper does not examine when row/column variance balancing fails (e.g., highly skewed activation distributions, layers with structured outliers), nor the interaction of dual scaling with joint weight-activation quantization, which is the setting where scale-vector placement in Eq. 6 may matter.

strengths: The core idea is simple, elegant, and well-motivated: dual-axis scaling factors allow trading quantization error between rows and columns of a weight tile, and the matrix imbalance (Eq. 4) is a plausible and novel proxy target. The modified Sinkhorn-Knopp iteration (Alg. 1) is an efficient way to optimize it, avoiding the sparse gradients that make the imbalance hard to optimize directly.

Empirical evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: the Qwen3 family from 0.6B to 235B-A22B, Llama 2/3, DeepSeek-V2.5 and DeepSeek-V3 (including MoE and MLA architectures), 3-bit and 4-bit settings, perplexity (WikiText2/C4), flip rates per Dutta et al. (2024), accuracy tables, and reasoning benchmarks with token-length controls (Tab. 6).
The runtime results are convincing and practically important: SINQ runs at ~1.1x RTN and ~2x faster than HQQ, while A-SINQ is ~8.5x RTN versus ~34-63x for AWQ/GPTQ (Tab. 7, 10 runs with std devs).

Good experimental hygiene: memory-fair Pareto analyses (Figs. 3-4) that account for auxiliary parameter overhead, ablations over tiling (1D/2D), shifts, and auxiliary precision, an explicit kurtosis-vs-imbalance comparison (Fig. 2) that justifies the proxy metric choice, and a fairness-matched HIGGS comparison (Tab. 11).

Demonstrated composability: SINQ combines with AWQ calibration (A-SINQ) and with non-uniform levels (SINQ-NF4), showing it is orthogonal to both axes, and the architecture-agnostic layer-local design is a genuine practical advantage over rotation-based methods.
Code availability and clearly specified default settings (group size 64, 1D tiling, dual-scale + shift) support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The theoretical grounding is thin: the imbalance metric is justified only empirically and heuristically. There is no analysis of convergence properties of the modified Sinkhorn iteration (with the max(sigma, sigma_min) clamping, log-domain accumulation, and early stopping all introduced in passing), nor an error-bound argument connecting imbalance minimization to weight MSE or end-to-end quality.

Gains at 4-bit over the strongest calibration-free baselines are modest (e.g., Qwen3-14B Wiki2: 8.76 vs. 8.78 for HQQ; Qwen3-32B: 7.74 vs. NF4's 7.94), and SINQ sometimes uses slightly more memory than HQQ/RTN baselines (e.g., 10.56 vs. 10.54 GB). The dramatic improvements are concentrated at 3-bit and on smaller models; the abstract's framing could acknowledge this more directly.

Calibrated comparisons are limited to GPTQ and AWQ; stronger calibrated or rotation-based systems (QuIP#, AQLM, SpinQuant, DuQuant as a baseline rather than related work) are not compared empirically, so the claim of 'approaching the quality of calibrated quantizers' is only established against a subset of the field.

The claimed speed advantage over HQQ ('faster... at > 2x') is not clearly consistent with the reported table, where SINQ averages 1.09x vs. HQQ's 2.32x relative to RTN; the wording in Sec. 3.4 is confusing.

Presentation issues: the code URL in the abstract is empty, some references are incomplete (Akhondzadeh et al. Kurtail lacks venue/year; SpinQuant entry lacks year; some author names abbreviated like 'Shao et al.' and 'Ma et al.' in the text), and there are minor typos ('inlcude').

Only weight-only quantization is evaluated; the interaction of dual output-side scales (t applied to activations per Eq. 6) with activation quantization or fused kernels is not studied, leaving some uncertainty about deployment behavior despite the stated motivation of compute-limited scenarios.

strengths: The central insight—that column-wise weight standard deviations are predictive of typical activation magnitudes—is novel, well-motivated (supported by both a simplified Adam-training analysis in Eq. 4/Fig. 2b and empirical R² evidence across Qwen, Llama, and Phi families in Fig. 6), and practically valuable because it enables calibration-free pseudo-activation-aware quantization.

The dual-scale parameterization combined with a dampened log-space Sinkhorn-Knopp iteration (Alg. 1) is simple, principled, and architecture-agnostic; the paper clearly articulates the row-kurtosis vs. column-scaling trade-off (Fig. 2c) that motivates balancing both axes rather than naively scaling columns.

Comprehensive and convincing evaluation: strong results on Qwen3 0.6B–235B, Llama, Phi, DeepSeek-V3/V2.5, and MoE models at 3/4-bit; SINQ often matches or exceeds calibrated methods (GPTQ, AWQ) without calibration (Tabs. 1–4), works with non-uniform formats (NF4, Tab. 3), and improves GGUF in llama.cpp (Tab. 9).

Thorough systems-level analysis: negligible inference overhead (Tab. 5, 1.8% worst case), near-RTN quantization time (1.09×, Tab. 10), end-to-end throughput in SGLang (Tab. 6), and a no-overhead variant; memory accounting is explicit and fair.

Good ablations (shifts, auxiliary precision, Pareto fronts in Fig. 5), reasoning benchmark results with trace-length analysis (Tab. 7), and permissively licensed code with open-source eval settings, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The theoretical underpinning of Eq. 4 is only observed in a highly simplified single-layer Gaussian setting; no formal derivation connects training dynamics to the general transformer case, leaving the pseudo-activation-awareness claim primarily empirical. A more rigorous analysis or discussion of when the correlation fails (e.g., heavily fine-tuned models, non-Adam training, narrow data regimes) would strengthen it.

Perplexity gains over the strongest calibration-free baselines (HQQ) shrink at larger scales (e.g., 4-bit 32B: 8.62 vs. 7.74 is strong, but 3-bit on 14B/32B gaps versus Hadamard+GPTQ are modest), and some headline claims of 'closing the gap' oversell the residual gap to BF16 at 3-bit for smaller models (e.g., 22.39 vs. 16.67 on Qwen3-1.7B).

Several key baseline results (RTN, Hadamard+RTN, Hadamard+GPTQ) are the authors' own implementations, and some algorithmic details (number of iterations K, step-size clamps smin/smax, sensitivity to these hyperparameters) are deferred to code rather than analyzed in the paper.

Evaluation relies mainly on perplexity and flip rates; downstream quality at very low bit-widths or for long-context/agentic settings is not examined, and there is no explicit limitations section discussing failure modes (e.g., the shared input-scale caveat in the no-overhead variant is described but its quality trade-off is relegated to an appendix).

Minor presentation issues: the code URL in the abstract is missing, and Fig. 1/2 are dense and would benefit from clearer captions; related-work comparisons to rotation-based W4 methods (QuaRot, SpinQuant, DuQuant) are qualitative only in the main text.

strengths: The paper identifies and empirically supports an interesting and somewhat surprising observation: column-wise weight standard deviations are predictive of typical activation magnitudes (Fig. 2a, Fig. 6 across Llama2, Phi, Qwen3 models), which enables a calibration-free approximation of activation-aware scaling. This is a genuinely useful insight for the calibration-free setting, where options are otherwise limited to RTN, HQQ, and Hadamard-based normalization.

The Sinkhorn-Knopp-style balancing of row and column standard deviations is a clean, principled mechanism for trading off the two competing error sources (activation-awareness vs. row-wise outlier creation), and the kurtosis analysis in Fig. 2c/3 gives concrete evidence for why the balancing matters.

The experimental coverage is broad: multiple model families (Qwen3, Llama, Phi, DeepSeek, MoE models up to 235B), 3-bit and 4-bit settings, uniform and non-uniform (NF4) formats, combination with AWQ/GPTQ, quantization-time and inference-overhead measurements, GGUF/llama.cpp and SGLang end-to-end results, and Pareto plots over the Qwen3 family. The reported inference overhead (1.8% worst case) and quantization time (~1.1x RTN) make the practical claims credible.
Reproducibility is treated well: full code is provided, evaluation settings follow an established external harness (Zheng et al., 2025), and permissively licensed open-weight models are used.
weaknesses: The core theoretical claim (Eq. 4, s_W proportional to 1/sqrt(|s_x|)) is only motivated by 'we observe' in a single simplified synthetic setting (one linear layer, Gaussian inputs, Adam). There is no derivation or analysis explaining when or why this relation should hold at scale, whether it depends on optimizer, training data distribution, or architecture, and no discussion of when it might fail. The 'pseudo-activation-awareness' framing rests largely on empirical correlation (R^2 values), and the cross-dataset 'upper bound' baseline in Fig. 2a is informal. This weakens the paper's central scientific claim beyond a useful heuristic.

Several headline claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The introduction asserts the paper 'largely closes the gap' between uncalibrated uniform quantization and calibrated/non-uniform approaches, yet Table 4 shows calibrated baselines (AWQ, Hadamard+GPTQ) remain competitive with or better than calibration-free SINQ at 3-bit on 14B/32B in several metrics, and Table 3 shows SINQ+NF4 still trails plain uniform SINQ nowhere consistently better than non-uniform baselines. The gap is narrowed, not closed.

Comparison fairness is uneven: several key baselines (RTN, Hadamard+RTN, Hadamard+GPTQ) are the authors' own implementations (marked dagger) with no external validation, and stronger recent calibration-free or transformation-based competitors (e.g., QuaRot/SpinQuant-style rotation pipelines in the calibration-free regime, Kurtail) are absent from the main tables, discussed only qualitatively. Perplexity numbers in Table 1 also look internally surprising (e.g., RTN at 3-bit on Qwen3-14B degrading Wiki2 only from 8.64 to 10.50, far better than Hadamard variants in some cells), which the paper does not explain or stress-test.

No variance reporting for the perplexity results: quantization pipelines have run-to-run variability (data ordering, implementation nondeterminism), and many reported wins are small (e.g., 4-bit Wiki2 deltas of 0.02-0.09 on 14B); without error bars or multiple seeds it is hard to distinguish real gains from noise. The 4-bit improvements on larger models in particular are marginal compared to the clear 3-bit wins.

Evaluation is dominated by perplexity and flip rates on three QA benchmarks. Downstream coverage is thin in the main text (reasoning results are preliminary pass@1 on AIME only, single model, and pushed to the appendix), and there is no analysis of sensitivity to hyperparameters such as the Sinkhorn step-size clamps (s_min, s_max), iteration count K, or failure modes on architectures whose weight/activation correlation is weaker.

Novelty is moderate: dual-axis scaling factors for quantization and iterative row/column normalization are each individually well-known ideas, and the combination, while effective and well-engineered, is an incremental contribution relative to prior transformations (Hadamard, SmoothQuant-style channel scaling). The paper's value depends substantially on the strength of the pseudo-activation-awareness insight, which as noted above is empirically but not theoretically grounded.

strengths: The core empirical finding — that column-wise weight standard deviations are predictive of input activation magnitudes (Fig. 2a, Fig. 6) — is genuinely interesting and enables calibration-free pseudo-activation-aware quantization, which is a novel angle relative to prior work that assumes calibration data is necessary for activation-awareness.

The method is simple, well-motivated, and practically attractive: layer-independent (unlike Hadamard/rotation methods), fast at quantization time (1.09x RTN, faster than HQQ), with negligible inference overhead (1.8% worst case, removable via the no-overhead variant).

The evaluation is unusually broad and thorough: Qwen3 family from 0.6B to 235B-A22B, Llama, Phi, DeepSeek-V2.5/V3 (including MoE and MLA architectures), uniform and non-uniform (NF4) quantization, combination with AWQ ('A-SINQ'), GGUF/llama.cpp end-to-end results, SGLang throughput, quantization-time distributions, and ablations on auxiliary precision and shifts.

The results are convincing where it matters: SINQ consistently dominates calibration-free baselines (RTN, Hadamard+RTN, HQQ, BnB, HIGGS) in Tables 1, 3, 11, 13, 19, and the uncalibrated variant often matches or beats calibrated GPTQ/AWQ (Table 4), which substantiates the headline claim of largely closing the calibration gap.

Good reproducibility posture: code in supplementary with permissive licensing, reliance on third-party open-source evaluation code (Zheng et al., 2025) for perplexity settings, openly licensed models, and memory usage reported to account for parameterization overhead differences.

The Sinkhorn-style balancing is a clean mechanism for trading off column normalization (pseudo-activation-awareness) against row kurtosis increase, and this trade-off is empirically validated (Figs. 2c, 3, 7).
weaknesses: The theoretical grounding for the central observation is informal. Equation 4 (s_W proportional to 1/sqrt(|s_x|)) is presented as an observed regularity in a toy single-layer Adam setup rather than derived, so the causal story behind the pseudo-activation-awareness remains speculative; the paper would benefit from at least a sketch of why the outer-product/Adam argument holds in multi-layer trained transformers.

A limitations section is absent. Relevant limitations (e.g., reliance on the std-dev/input-scale correlation possibly being an artifact of common training recipes and thus fragile for non-standard training, shared input scales in the no-overhead variant trading quality for speed, and the remaining 3-bit gap on small models such as Qwen3-1.7B: 22.39 vs. 16.67 BF16) are only implicit.

Margins over strong baselines are sometimes small: at 4-bit, A-SINQ vs. AWQ/GPTQ differences in flips and perplexity are frequently within ~0.02-0.1 (Tables 2, 4), and no variance estimates or significance tests are reported for perplexity/flip results, so some 'best in bold' claims are within noise.

Baseline fairness relies on authors' own implementations for several key comparisons (RTN, Hadamard+RTN, Hadamard+GPTQ, marked with daggers); while open-source eval code mitigates this, the manuscript gives few details on how these baselines were tuned.

Reasoning results (Table 7) are explicitly preliminary pass@1 on AIME with small problem counts, which cannot support strong conclusions; the text appropriately hedges, but this limits the downstream-task evidence beyond perplexity/flips.

Presentation issues: several references are incomplete (Shao et al., Liu et al., Sun et al., Akhondzadeh et al. lack years/venues), and the abstract's 'Code is available at' sentence is truncated, indicating insufficient final polishing.

Novelty is incremental at the component level: dual (row/column) transformations exist in SmoothQuant/DuQuant, and weight-space transformations are well studied; the novelty lies mainly in the calibration-free derivation of scales from weight statistics plus the Sinkhorn balancing, which reviewers should weigh when judging significance.
